A Chinese novel of the Ming dynasty, first printed in 1592, that tells of the monk Tang Sanzang's pilgrimage to India to fetch Buddhist scriptures, guarded by the Monkey King and other magical disciples. It is one of the four classic novels of Chinese literature and perhaps the most popular book in East Asia.

The story is based on a real journey. The Tang monk Xuanzang travelled to India from 629 and came back seventeen years later with hundreds of texts, and wrote an account of the lands he saw. Storytellers and playwrights turned his trip into legend over the following centuries. The novel gathered these tales into a hundred chapters. It is usually credited to Wu Cheng'en, though the book appeared without an author's name and his authorship is debated.

The cast:

  • Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, born from a stone, who masters 72 transformations and wreaks havoc in heaven before the Buddha traps him under a mountain.
  • Zhu Bajie, a greedy, lazy pig spirit.
  • Sha Wujing, a quiet river ogre.
  • A dragon prince turned into the monk's white horse.

Along the way they face eighty-one ordeals and countless demons who want to eat the monk.

The book mixes adventure and comedy with Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian ideas, and can be read as a story of the mind learning discipline. Arthur Waley's 1942 English version, Monkey, made it known in the West. It still feeds films, television, comics and games, from Dragon Ball to Black Myth: Wukong.
